arXiv:2607.27275v1 [cs.LG] 29 Jul 2026

Flat Score, Amplified Failures:
How the Error Budget Masks Damage in Quantized LLM Agents

Jiwon Jang    Kisu Yang    Heuiseok Lim\corresponding    Hyunwoo Park\corresponding
Abstract

Post-training quantization to 4-bit weights is widely reported to be nearly lossless. We test this claim for multi-turn, tool-calling agents, where it now matters most. On τ2\tau^{2}-bench, across two open-weight model families in dense and MoE variants and two domains (eight cells, 456 episodes each, at 16-, 8-, and 4-bit weights), quantization indeed looks free on the standard metric. No cell shows a score change that survives multiple-comparison correction, and in the cell that carries the largest process damage, equivalence testing bounds the change within ±7.5\pm 7.5 points. The process tells a different story. Quantization amplifies the failure the model already exhibits at full precision (tool-name hallucination in telecom, with the same directional trend in retail entity errors) by up to 2.5×2.5\times in volume (+17.6+17.6 points per task), while creating essentially no new failures. The failure set is the same at every precision (rank correlation ≥0.94\geq 0.94, 0.18%0.18\% novel events). The score stays flat because the benchmark’s ten-error budget absorbs the extra failures. Shrinking the budget to two errors re-exposes a score gap of 1717 points, and it does so only in the one cell where quantization added error volume, exactly as the masking account predicts. A targeted error-repair prompt, run for five telecom models at every precision, removes the damage exactly and only where it lives. Both diagnostics, the per-channel error rate and success under a shrinking budget, come from logs benchmarks already collect; we suggest reporting them alongside task reward.

Introduction

Weight quantization is the default mechanism for serving large language models (LLMs) at scale. Reducing weights from 16 to 4 bits cuts memory and latency several-fold, and systematic evaluations report 4-bit quantization as nearly lossless, degrading standard benchmark accuracy by only a point or two (Frantar et al. 2023; Lin et al. 2024; Li et al. 2024b; Jin et al. 2024). That verdict, however, rests almost entirely on single-turn evaluations, while deployed LLMs increasingly act as agents, multi-turn tool-calling controllers that interact with an environment, observe feedback, and recover from their own mistakes.

RQ1: Does “nearly lossless” survive the shift to multi-turn tool-calling agents, and can the benchmark’s final score tell? The natural way to ask turns out to be misleading. The obvious experiment is to run quantized and full-precision agents on an agentic benchmark and compare task success. We do exactly this on τ2\tau^{2}-bench (Barres et al. 2026), a tool-calling benchmark with a simulated user, across two open-weight model families ×\times {dense, MoE} ×\times two domains (the full eight-cell grid, 456 simulations per arm), plus two earlier Qwen-3.5 checkpoints in telecom. The result is a flat line (Figure 1a). No score change survives multiple-comparison correction, and the largest paired decline, 2.02.0 points, sits within 1.3×1.3\times the run-to-run noise floor. Taken at face value, quantization is free in the agentic setting too. Compression studies of agents have so far stopped at this aggregate verdict (Dong et al. 2025); the rest of the paper asks what it conceals.

We argue this conclusion is an artifact of what task reward measures. Task reward is a binary, end-of-trajectory outcome. It is swamped by task-difficulty variance and, more importantly, the agentic loop actively repairs the errors quantization introduces before they reach the outcome. Decomposed at the level of individual tool calls, trajectories instead reveal a large effect with two parts. First, universally, quantization does not change what the model gets wrong. In telecom, where the channel is tool-name hallucination (calls outside the agent’s tool list, nearly always real tools on the user’s side of the dual-control interface), the BF16 and INT4 distributions over hallucinated names are nearly identical, and the invariance holds at 8 bits. The failure set is a property of the model, not of any precision. Second, in a cell-dependent way, quantization multiplies how often that set fires. In the highest-amplification cell (Gemma-4 dense, telecom), 4-bit weights produce 2.5×2.5\times more out-of-list calls (→1,646649\!\to\!1{,}646); across cells the multiplier ranges from ≈1×{\approx}1\times to 4.6×4.6\times, and in retail the channel that moves is entity/argument errors instead (1.45×1.45\times, Gemma-4 MoE, a trend short of significance). Quantization rescales the model’s existing error set; the scale factor is a property of the cell.

RQ2: Why does the final score stay flat while the agent’s per-step failures multiply? Because the loop hides the damage. τ2\tau^{2}-bench, like other agentic benchmarks, allows ten failed tool calls per episode, and per-error recovery is equally reliable at both precisions, so the budget absorbs the extra failures quantization produces. Tightening the tolerance from ten errors to two re-exposes the deficit, growing the INT4 score gap from 1.31.3 to 16.716.7 points, and it re-exposes damage only in the one cell where quantization added error volume (15.415.4 points there, at most 0.20.2 elsewhere). The score is flat because the environment is forgiving, not because the model is unharmed. The same localization predicts the remedy, and a reflexive error-repair prompt indeed collapses the channel wherever it runs but moves score only in the damaged cell.

RQ3: Why are some models damaged by quantization while others are unaffected? Not size or dense-versus-MoE architecture but the model’s full-precision failure propensity. A model that rarely hallucinates tools at 16 bits (Qwen-3.6) has nothing to amplify, a model with a standing tendency (Gemma-4) has that tendency magnified, and an older Qwen-3.5 checkpoint whose gate is slightly open is slightly, but significantly, amplified. The open gate is necessary rather than sufficient, since a cell with an equally open gate (Gemma-4 MoE telecom, 19.3%19.3\%) multiplies by only 1.05×1.05\times. A logit-margin account is consistent with this pattern. Quantization noise flips only thin-margin argmax decisions, precisely those the model already got wrong occasionally, making baseline propensity the observable shadow of the thin-margin mass.

Our contributions are:

  • •

    The final score cannot detect 4-bit damage (RQ1). End-of-episode task reward is not merely low-powered but actively masked by the environment’s error budget; stopping at task success yields a false “all-clear.”

  • •

    Quantization amplifies the existing failure set (RQ1). (i) The failure set is precision-invariant across 16, 8, and 4 bits (0.970.97 correlation, 0.18%0.18\% novel events), ruling out the “some models are just worse” confound; (ii) the failure volume multiplier is cell-dependent, 1×1\times to 4.6×4.6\times, so damage claims must be made per cell.

  • •

    The error budget masks the damage, falsifiably (RQ2). A counterfactual budget analysis shows the recovery slack hides the damage; its advance prediction, that tightening re-exposes damage only in cells with added error volume, holds across all cells (one adds volume, nine check the converse), widening 15.415.4 points there versus at most 0.20.2 elsewhere; and a reflexive error-repair system, run for five telecom models at all three precisions, recovers score only in the damaged cell.

  • •

    Full-precision propensity gates the risk (RQ3). Neither architecture nor size does. A standing full-precision failure channel is the precondition, and the added error volume the observable signature, of maskable damage. Both come from logs benchmarks already collect; we suggest reporting them alongside task reward, and low-slack deployments face more 4-bit risk than single-turn benchmarks show.

Related Work

Post-training quantization and its evaluation.

Post-training weight quantization (Frantar et al. 2023; Lin et al. 2024; Xiao et al. 2023; Dettmers et al. 2022) has become the default mechanism for serving large language models, and systematic evaluations consistently report that 4-bit quantization leaves aggregate benchmark accuracy largely intact (Li et al. 2024b; Jin et al. 2024). A separate line of work, however, shows that this aggregate view conceals non-uniform damage. Compression disproportionately affects long-tail and underrepresented inputs (Hooker et al. 2019; Ahia et al. 2021), increases hallucination rates in generation (Li et al. 2024a; Haque et al. 2025), and can erode alignment- and safety-related behaviors (Rath and Maliakkal 2026). These studies establish that quantization damage hides below aggregate metrics, but in single-turn, static generation; none characterize where it goes in a closed-loop agentic trajectory, nor why end-to-end metrics stay flat while per-step reliability degrades.

Evaluating tool-calling agents.

Benchmarks for tool use have progressed from single-turn function calling (Patil et al. 2024), function-calling leaderboards (Patil et al. 2025), and stepwise capability probes (Chen et al. 2024; Qin et al. 2024) to long-horizon interactive environments with simulated users, most notably τ\tau-bench (Yao et al. 2025) and its dual-control successor τ2\tau^{2}-bench (Barres et al. 2026). These environments score agents by end-of-episode task reward (pass^kk), and prior analyses note that tool use is fragile (Cuadron et al. 2026), yet the benchmarks ship with generous per-episode error tolerances allowing retries. All of this work evaluates full-precision models; the interaction of error tolerance with per-step error rate has not been examined as a measurement problem.

Compression under agentic workloads.

Closest to our setting, Dong et al. (2025) evaluate quantized and pruned models on agentic capability suites and report capability-level degradation patterns, and Paramanayakam et al. (2025) document performance drops when quantized models serve as on-device function-calling agents. Both efforts score isolated steps or aggregate accuracy on a fixed pipeline. We instead evaluate quantized agents closed-loop across single- and dual-control domains, decompose failures into domain-specific channels, and trace individual failure events across precisions within a single model, yielding two findings unavailable to step-level or aggregate evaluation. Quantization amplifies the model’s pre-existing failure set rather than creating new failures, and the final score is blind to the amplification because the environment’s error budget absorbs the extra failures until that budget is tightened.

Experimental Setup

Benchmark.

We evaluate on τ2\tau^{2}-bench (Barres et al. 2026), a tool-calling benchmark in which an agent resolves a customer request over a multi-turn conversation with a simulated user, issuing tool calls against a stateful environment. We use its two domains. Retail is a single-control setting in which only the agent acts on the environment; telecom is a dual-control setting in which the user also executes actions on their own device and the agent must reason about state it cannot manipulate directly. The domains differ in horizon and tool inventory (telecom trajectories are longer, median ∼\sim16 versus ∼\sim11 agent turns, with a larger, less standard tool set) and, as we show, expose different failure channels. Each domain contains 114 tasks; an episode ends when the user closes the conversation, when the agent exhausts max_errors=10{=}10 failed tool calls, or at max_steps=300{=}300. Task reward is the standard τ2\tau^{2}-bench outcome (a final database-state check plus per-task assertions). In practice it is binary in both domains, so we report its mean as the final score in percent.

Models and quantization.

We study two open-weight LLM families, each in a dense and a mixture-of-experts (MoE) variant, namely Gemma-4-31B (dense) and Gemma-4-26B-A4B (MoE, 4B active parameters), and Qwen-3.6-27B (dense) and Qwen-3.6-35B-A3B (MoE, 3B active parameters), plus Qwen-3.5-27B and Qwen-3.5-9B (both dense) as family-version and size extensions. Each model runs at three precision arms: BF16, the original 16-bit weights and full-precision reference; FP8; and INT4, quantized with AWQ. All agents are served with vLLM on NVIDIA A100 GPUs; the A100 has no native FP8 compute, so the FP8 weights run weight-only via the Marlin kernel (W8A16). Activations and the KV cache are 16-bit in every arm; all three arms are weight-only. Recipes differ by family (AWQ-style with g=32g{=}32 for Gemma INT4, zero-point AWQ with g=128g{=}128 for Qwen INT4). The full cross-product (two families ×\times {dense, MoE} ×\times two domains, eight cells) is complete at all three precisions, with both Qwen-3.5 telecom extensions on top. Episodes terminated by infrastructure_error (≤3\leq 3 per arm) carry no reward record and are excluded (one retail cell mixed max_steps of 200 and 300; no episode reaches either cap).

Protocol.

To isolate the effect of agent quantization, the simulated user is held fixed at full precision (Qwen-3.6-27B, BF16) across all conditions; only the agent’s precision varies. In the Qwen-3.6 dense cells the agent thus shares a base model with the user simulator; the Qwen-3.5 and Qwen-3.6 MoE cells, which do not, behave identically, so this does not drive the family contrast. We run num_trials=4{=}4 trials per task, giving 114×4=456114\times 4=456 simulations per cell. vLLM serving is not bit-deterministic (continuous batching perturbs reduction order); a repeated 456-episode run shifted the mean score by about 1.51.5 points, our coarse single-repeat estimate of the run-to-run noise floor. Unless noted, comparisons are BF16 versus INT4 within a fixed model and domain, holding family, architecture, task distribution, and user simulator constant.

Process metrics and failure channels.

Beyond task reward, we log every tool call and its outcome. Our primary process metric is the channel rate, the fraction of the agent’s own tool calls (user-simulator calls excluded) that trigger a given failure channel, pooled over a cell; paired tests use the same rate computed per task. We decompose failures into two channels by matching the environment’s error string. A tool-name hallucination is a call to a tool that does not exist in the domain’s inventory (error Tool ’XX’ not found); this is the dominant channel in telecom. An entity/argument error is a well-formed call whose arguments reference a record that cannot be found (e.g. a wrong customer or order identifier); this is the channel in retail. A raw “not found” count would conflate inventing a tool with passing a wrong identifier, and the two behave differently. We additionally track trajectory length (agent turns, tool calls), termination reasons, and, for the mechanism analysis, the per-task and per-tool-name distributions of hallucinations.

Statistics.

For each metric we report the change from BF16 to INT4 with a 95% confidence interval from 5,0005{,}000 bootstrap resamples. Because the four trials of a task share its difficulty, we resample tasks with replacement, keeping all trials of each sampled task (a cluster bootstrap over the 114 tasks); an interval excluding zero denotes significance. Episode-level resampling gives narrower intervals; we report clustered intervals throughout. Paired-by-task comparisons (removing task-difficulty variance) and equivalence tests (two one-sided tests, TOST) at ±7.5\pm 7.5 points supplement these where noted. For the mechanism analysis we compute, within one model×\timesdomain, the BF16/INT4 correlation of hallucinated-name distributions, the fraction of INT4 events unseen at BF16, and the per-task BF16/INT4 rate relationship.

Repair arm.

For the mitigation study, five telecom models (the grid’s four plus Qwen-3.5-27B) are additionally run at every precision with a reflexive repair loop: on a failed tool call, the agent is prompted to diagnose the error message and re-issue a corrected call, up to three attempts. Agent decoding is greedy in all arms (verified from the logs: identical prefixes always yield identical outputs); repair arms differ from base only in user-simulator temperature, 0.60.6 versus 0.70.7, so we read contrasts against the run-to-run noise floor.

Counterfactual error budget.

To ask whether the environment’s error tolerance hides the damage, we treat max_errors as a knob. For a budget KK, the surviving success rate S⁡(K)S(K) is the fraction of episodes that succeeded using at most KK failed tool calls. The projection is conservative (an episode exceeding KK counts as a failure even if it finished earlier) but applied identically to both precisions, so the gap SBF16​(K)−SINT4​(K)S_{\text{BF16}}(K)-S_{\text{INT4}}(K) is a fair comparison; too_many_errors terminations occur at 10–11 counted errors, confirming KK matches max_errors.

Results

Final Task Reward Is Blind to Quantization

Table 1 (left) and Figure 1a report the change in the final score from 16- to 4-bit weights. In all ten cells the 95% interval includes zero; the largest point estimate is 4.64.6 points and five cells nominally improve. The absence of a difference is not merely low power. In seven cells, including the highest-signal one below, the change is statistically equivalent to zero by TOST at ±7.5\pm 7.5 points, paired by task. In the three remaining Gemma-4 cells the intervals are wider than the margin, so flatness there means no detectable change, not equivalence. The largest paired decline, 2.02.0 points in Qwen-3.6 MoE telecom at p=.049p{=}.049, survives neither multiple-comparison correction nor the 1.51.5-point noise floor and lies well inside the equivalence margin. Paired by task in the highest-signal cell, 4-bit is worse on 33 tasks, better on 26, tied on 55. Aggregate or paired, task success cannot distinguish a 4-bit agent from a full-precision one; the rest of this section shows why that all-clear is wrong.

The Damage Is Real, in the Process, and Channel-Specific

When we decompose trajectories into the two failure channels (Table 1, right, and Figure 1b), a large and systematic effect emerges. In telecom, whose active channel is tool-name hallucination, 4-bit quantization raises the Gemma-4 dense hallucination rate from 19.5%19.5\% to 38.3%38.3\% of the agent’s tool calls (+18.8{+}18.8 points, CI [14.0,23.6][14.0,23.6]), a 2.0×2.0\times increase, and drives a 9×9\times rise in error-budget-exhausting terminations (→465\!\to\!46 of 456 episodes). Because INT4 trajectories also contain more calls per episode (→9.47.3\!\to\!9.4), the 2.0×2.0\times rate ratio is a 2.5×2.5\times growth in event volume (→1,646649\!\to\!1{,}646), the multiplier we quote. In retail, whose active channel is entity/argument errors, the same family moves in that channel instead (Gemma-4 MoE, 4.2%→5.7%4.2\%\!\rightarrow\!5.7\%, +1.5{+}1.5, CI [−0.1,+3.1][-0.1,+3.1], a trend short of significance under clustered intervals). Whichever failure the domain makes available, quantization pushes on it in Gemma-4. The channel structure is sharp. Retail produces zero tool-name events and telecom entity rates stay ≤0.1%{\leq}0.1\%. Each domain opens exactly one failure mode, and quantization can only amplify an open channel.

Three observations sharpen the picture. First, Qwen-3.6 is not amplified in any of its four cells. Telecom tool-name stays at 0.38%→0.47%0.38\%\!\to\!0.47\%, not significant, with 9 events at BF16, and retail entity rates are flat. Second, architecture is not a stand-alone predictor. The one strongly amplified cell is dense, yet the dense Qwen-3.6 is flat everywhere, and the Gemma-4 MoE shows only non-significant trends (+3.8{+}3.8 points in telecom, +1.5{+}1.5 in retail), so dense-versus-MoE by itself does not sort damaged from undamaged cells. Third, susceptibility is checkpoint-specific. The previous-generation Qwen-3.5, whose gate is slightly open (0.26%0.26\%), is significantly amplified (→1.21%\rightarrow 1.21\%, +0.95{+}0.95 [0.5,1.5][0.5,1.5]), Gemma-4’s pattern at a twentieth of the magnitude, while its successor and its smaller 9B sibling (gate 0.61%0.61\%) are both flat. The discriminating variable is the model’s own baseline behavior, not size or architecture (§ Analysis).

The Cliff Is (Mostly) at Four Bits

Sweeping the intermediate precision shows that 8 bits, weight-only in our serving setup, is close to free. No cell degrades significantly in score (one nominally improves by 9.79.7 points; with ten cells tested, one excursion is unsurprising) and no telecom channel moves at FP8; the jump to 38.3%38.3\% happens entirely between 8 and 4 bits. One trend is instructive. Gemma-4 MoE retail already shows its full INT4-sized entity/argument movement at FP8 (+1.40{+}1.40, CI [−0.2,3.0][-0.2,3.0], not significant under clustered intervals). If that trend is real, the safe-precision boundary, too, is a property of the model×\timeschannel pair, not a universal constant.

Quantization Amplifies the Existing Failure Set, Not New Ones

Is the damage a new pathology or a scaling-up of what the model already did? We answer within a single model and domain, Gemma-4 dense telecom, removing any family or architecture confound.

At the level of individual tool names, quantization is almost purely multiplicative (Figure 2a). The set of hallucinated tool names is essentially unchanged. The per-tool frequency distributions at BF16 and INT4 correlate at 0.970.97, only 3 of the 1,6461{,}646 INT4 hallucinations (0.18%0.18\%) invoke a tool that was never invented at BF16, and the top-15 fabricated tools at BF16 are all present at INT4, invoked 2.5×2.5\times more often (→1,646649\!\rightarrow\!1{,}646 total). Quantization does not make the model imagine new tools; it makes it reach more often for the ones it was already tempted by.

The invented names are not fabrications. Of the 24 distinct hallucinated names, 23 are real tools on the user’s side of the dual-control interface (toggle_airplane_mode, run_speed_test, …; the 24th is a near-miss of the user-side check_sim_status), covering 99.8%99.8\% of BF16 and 100%100\% of INT4 events. The channel is role-boundary confusion, the agent reaching for actions only the user can perform, and quantization amplifies that pre-existing confusion; retail’s structural zero follows, having no user side to reach across.

At the level of tasks, the amplification takes the form of a near-uniform shift rather than a proportional scaling (Figure 2b). Regressing the per-task increase on the task’s full-precision rate gives a slope of −0.06{-}0.06, indistinguishable from zero. The increase is a constant +17.6{+}17.6 points regardless of where the task started (tercile means +18.1+18.1, +17.2+17.2, +17.4+17.4); the pooled rise is the slightly larger +18.8{+}18.8 points because tasks contribute unequal call counts. The propensity signal is therefore strongest as a gate, whether the model opens this failure mode at all (649 baseline events in Gemma-4 telecom, 9 in Qwen-3.6 telecom, 0 in the retail tool-name channel), rather than as fine per-task proportionality. Either way, quantization scales an existing failure distribution rather than creating a new one.

Why the Score Stays Flat: the Error Budget Masks It

Sections above leave a puzzle. If per-step failures rise 2.5×2.5\times, why is the final score unchanged? Because the agentic loop recovers the extra failures, and the benchmark’s error budget pays for the recovery (Table 2). Two facts establish this. First, quantization raises failed tool calls per episode from 1.451.45 to 3.643.64 (2.5×2.5\times), swelling the ≥5{\geq}5-failure tail from 51 to 173 of 456 episodes (Figure 4) and stretching trajectories (→17.916.4\!\to\!17.9 turns, →9.47.3\!\to\!9.4 calls; errors–turns r=0.48r{=}0.48), error-driven recovery that quietly refunds part of the compute quantization saved. Second, the model recovers from each individual failure about equally well at both precisions. The recovery rate after at least one failed call is 55%55\% at both BF16 and INT4. Quantization does not weaken recovery; it simply produces more failures to recover from, and the 1010-error budget absorbs them.

Treating that budget as a knob makes the masking explicit and falsifiable (Figure 3). Recomputing the surviving success rate S⁡(K)S(K) under tighter budgets, the score gap between BF16 and INT4 grows as KK shrinks. It is 1.31.3 points at the default K=10K{=}10, then 7.57.5 at K=5K{=}5 and 16.716.7 at K=2K{=}2, roughly a 13×13\times widening; the same tightening costs BF16 1010 points but INT4 2525. The Qwen-3.6-27B cell is a negative control. With almost no baseline failures, masking predicts no hidden gap there, and indeed it is flat at every KK, nothing for a tighter budget to expose.

The budget response doubles as a falsification test. If masking explains the flat score, tightening should re-expose damage only where quantization added error volume. Across all cells this is exactly what happens. The gap widens by 15.415.4 points in Gemma-4 dense telecom, the one cell with a large added volume, while no other cell widens by more than 0.20.2 points. The largest movement elsewhere is a 2.22.2-point narrowing in Gemma-4 MoE telecom, whose event volume grows only about 5%5\%. Where nothing was hidden, nothing is revealed. The score is flat because the environment is forgiving, and the damage re-emerges precisely where, and only where, it exists. The test is not vacuous, since extra failures landing in episodes already lost would re-expose nothing, and this partly happens. All 46 INT4 exhaustions score zero yet the default-budget gap is only 1.31.3 points, so part of the damage lands in episodes lost anyway. With one volume-adding cell the positive arm has a single member; the eight flat cells check the converse, and a rerun at a tightened budget is the decisive version of the test.

Why Quantization Amplifies Existing Failures

A logit-margin account.

The amplify-but-do-not-invent pattern of Figure 2 follows from a simple property of quantized decoding. At any generation step, let the model choose among tokens by their logits, and consider the correct token cc and its strongest competitor ww, with margin m=zc−zwm=z_{c}-z_{w}. Weight quantization perturbs the logits by approximately zero-mean noise η\eta, so the post-quantization margin is m′=m+ηm^{\prime}=m+\eta. The probability that the argmax flips (that the model now errs) changes by Δp(m)=𝔼η[σ(−(m+η)/τ)]−σ(−m/τ)\Delta p(m)=\mathbb{E}_{\eta}[\sigma(-(m+\eta)/\tau)]-\sigma(-m/\tau) for a temperature-like scale τ\tau. It is near zero for large positive mm (confident decisions) and large negative mm (already lost), and maximized near m≈0m\approx 0. Quantization damage therefore concentrates on thin-margin decisions.

Two predictions follow, both borne out. First, a thin-margin flip promotes the already-closest competitor, the failure the model occasionally made anyway, so quantization reuses the existing failure set (0.970.97 correlation, 0.18%0.18\% novel). Second, baseline error rate and quantization-induced increase are governed by the same latent quantity, the mass of thin-margin decisions, so a model’s full-precision failure rate is the observable shadow of its quantization sensitivity; the prediction is not circular, being tested at a finer grain, the per-tool-name distribution, than the aggregate rate it predicts. A positional test separates this account from a natural alternative in which quantization erodes instruction-following as the context grows. That account predicts damage concentrated late, but the INT4-to-BF16 ratio stays within 1.3×1.3\times–2.0×2.0\times in every turn bin and the hallucination rate falls in the longest-context quartile at both precisions.

What governs susceptibility.

The account explains the family split. Qwen-3.6 adheres almost perfectly to the tool schema at full precision (0.38%0.38\%, 9 events). It has essentially no thin-margin mass here and nothing to amplify, genuinely robust rather than merely saturated, as the process metric confirms. Gemma-4 carries a standing tendency to invent plausible tools (649 events), and quantization magnifies exactly that tendency. The claim is not “Gemma is worse” but “quantization scales up whatever a model is already prone to.” Architecture does not set this propensity; the checkpoint does. The Qwen releases have near-zero baselines (0.26%0.26\% versus 0.38%0.38\%) yet land on opposite sides of significance (+0.95{+}0.95 versus +0.09{+}0.09 points), so near the closed end the gate pins the ceiling, damage near 1%1\% versus 38%38\% where it is wide open, rather than the exact magnitude. The converse is sharper than raw counts suggest. Gemma-4 MoE telecom opens the gate as wide per call as the dense variant (19.3%19.3\% versus 19.5%19.5\% at BF16, 841 events) yet multiplies by only 1.05×1.05\times, per-tool factors scattering 0.5×0.5\times–1.5×1.5\times instead of the dense 2.5×2.5\times. The gate is necessary for large damage, not sufficient; the aggregate rate cannot see the thin-margin mass, which varies by cell. The domain contrast follows the same logic. Telecom’s dual-control split places plausible device actions just across the agent/user role boundary, creating thin-margin choices between near-synonymous agent- and user-side names; single-control retail has no boundary and a structurally zero tool-name channel.

Discussion

Agentic benchmarks need process-level reporting.

End-of-episode reward is blind to quantization for a structural reason. It is a saturating outcome buffered by the environment’s error tolerance, so a benchmark reporting only task reward certifies a compressed agent whose per-step reliability has halved. Benchmarks should report per-channel error rates alongside task reward and, where an error budget exists, success as a function of that budget; both come from existing logs and are far more sensitive.

Full-precision propensity is a cheap risk screen.

Susceptibility is governed by full-precision propensity, so risk can be screened before quantizing by measuring the per-channel error rate on the target domain. A near-zero rate, as for Qwen-3.6, signals 4-bit is likely safe there. The screen is one-directional, an elevated rate flagging risk without pinning the multiplier, since an equally open gate can stay flat (Gemma-4 MoE telecom); it still beats size and architecture.

Deployment slack is not always benchmark slack.

The masking depends on a forgiving environment. Many real deployments are not forgiving, with single-shot interactions, strict error limits, irreversible actions, and no silent retries. With the slack gone, amplified per-step failures become outcome failures, as the budget-tightening analysis projects. “Lossless on the benchmark” need not be lossless where deployed.

A mechanism-targeted mitigation.

The damage is amplification of a small, enumerable set the model already produces at full precision, with 99.8%99.8\% of INT4 hallucinations repeating BF16 tool names, so the remedy is forbidding that set at the source rather than general robustness. Constrained decoding, native in vLLM, eliminates the dominant channel by restricting the tool-name field to the inventory. We run the lighter reflexive repair system of Setup for five telecom models at all precisions; the one significant gain is the damaged cell, Gemma-4 dense at INT4, +5.9{+}5.9 points (CI [+1.1,+10.8][+1.1,+10.8], p=.017p{=}.017) to 71.3%71.3\%, above unmitigated BF16 (66.7%66.7\%), while every other interval includes zero. The mechanism is prevention rather than cure. The in-context inventory collapses the out-of-list volume from 1,6461{,}646 events to 8282 and shortens trajectories (→15.917.9\!\to\!15.9 turns). Both negative controls behave. Qwen cells, with nothing to repair, move within or near the ±2.0\pm 2.0-point repeat-run band, and repair trends negative only where nothing needs fixing (Gemma-4 MoE, whose score dip is not channel-mediated, −2.6-2.6 at BF16 and −4.2-4.2 at INT4; Qwen-3.6 −2.4-2.4 at FP8; none significant). The same prompt suppresses its errors only 4×4\times (→217882\!\to\!217) versus 20×20\times dense, and its trajectories lengthen. Help only where the channel damage lives, nothing where nothing needs fixing, mild harm elsewhere, a third confirmation of the localization. The fix is per-channel. Retail’s entity/argument errors instead call for validate-and-retry or argument grounding, the propensity screen deciding when either is needed.

Beyond quantization.

Nothing in the logit-margin account is specific to quantization. Any weight perturbation adding near-zero-mean logit noise (pruning, low-rank compression, distillation drift) should likewise amplify existing thin-margin failures, not create new ones. The agentic loop accumulates and hides such damage, making multi-turn tool use a probe for perturbations single-turn accuracy misses.

Conclusion

Standard evaluations call 4-bit quantization nearly lossless, and our ten agentic cells agree, with no final-score change surviving correction. The agreement is an artifact of what the score can see. Underneath, quantization amplifies the failures the model already exhibits, the same tools invented more often, up to 2.5×2.5\times while creating almost nothing new. The benchmark’s error budget absorbs the extra failures, and tightening it re-exposes the damage exactly where, and only where, it was added, and a channel-targeted repair recovers the score there. Susceptibility follows the model’s own full-precision propensity, not its size or architecture. Measure process, not just outcome.

Appendix A Additional Results

Figure 5 visualizes the precision sweep BF16→\toFP8→\toINT4 for every cell of the paper’s grid; Table 4 reports the BF16→\rightarrowFP8 comparison under the main protocol. Figure 6 tests whether the amplification depends on position in the trajectory. Table 3 reports the full repair grid behind the mitigation paragraph of the Discussion, and a closing paragraph disentangles three conflated senses of “horizon.”

Horizon is three things, pulling in opposite directions.

“Longer horizons hurt more” conflates three quantities that act oppositely. The task horizon, the decisions a task requires, generates damage, since more decisions expose more thin-margin steps (telecom, median ∼\sim16 turns, shows the effect; retail, ∼\sim11, does not). The budget horizon (max_errors) hides it, as the loop recovers the amplified failures until the tolerance is tightened. Realized trajectory length is neither, being a downstream symptom of recovery, driven by errors (r=0.48r{=}0.48).

Appendix B Limitations

The paper’s strongest claims are within-model, robust to the family confound; four limitations bound the generalization. (i) Two families plus two further Qwen checkpoints support the propensity claim as a gate, open versus closed, not a fitted curve; a curve needs more checkpoints. (ii) The budget-masking result is a projection from existing trajectories, conservative by construction; a rerun at tightened budgets would confirm it directly, and the margin account is likewise indirect, since token log-probabilities are not in our logs, though Figure 6 rules out the leading alternative. (iii) The INT4 recipes differ between families (Table 6), partly conflating checkpoint with recipe; the confound is bounded, since the finer-grouped, normally more accurate recipe belongs to the amplified family and the recipe-matched Qwen-3.5/3.6 pair is separated by baseline propensity alone, but a same-recipe requantization is the missing control. (iv) Our evidence spans one benchmark, two domains, and weight-only recipes on A100 GPUs with a 16-bit KV cache, a fixed full-precision user simulator, and a telecom-only repair arm; low-bit KV caches, activation-quantized FP8, other benchmarks, and compressed user simulators are open.

Appendix C Reproducibility Details

Benchmark and protocol.

All runs use a single τ2\tau^{2}-bench commit with its standard retail and telecom domains (114 tasks each), num_trials=4{=}4, seed 300300, max_steps=300{=}300, max_errors=10{=}10, agent sampling temperature 0.00.0, and user-simulator temperature 0.70.7 (0.60.6 in the repair arms, which also set an explicit agent seed). One nonuniformity remains. The Gemma-4-31B retail arms ran at max_steps=200{=}200 (BF16, INT4) and 300300 (FP8); no episode in any arm reaches either cap, so the difference is immaterial. The user simulator is Qwen-3.6-27B at BF16 in every arm, served as a separate vLLM instance; only the agent model and its precision vary across cells.

Serving.

Agents are served with vLLM on NVIDIA A100 GPUs with a 16-bit KV cache. Because the A100 has no native FP8 compute, vLLM executes the FP8 checkpoints as weight-only 8-bit via the Marlin kernel (W8A16); the dynamic per-token activation quantization specified in the FP8 configurations is therefore inactive, and activations are 16-bit in all three arms.

Quantization configurations.

Table 6 lists each arm’s weight-quantization recipe as read from the served checkpoints’ quantization_config.

Coincidence note.

The identical score triples of the Qwen-3.6-35B-A3B and Qwen-3.5-27B telecom rows in Table 1 are a counting coincidence. Both cells succeed in 448 of 456 episodes at BF16 and 439 at INT4, while the underlying episode outcomes differ in 16 and 32 episodes respectively.

Analysis.

Every number in the paper is computed from the raw simulation logs by a single analysis script (channel regexes, per-cell bootstrap and paired tests, S⁡(K)S(K) projection, and figure/table generation); the script and per-episode logs will be released upon publication.

Appendix D Sample Trajectories

The channel rates in the paper are computed by pattern-matching the per-episode logs. This section grounds that measurement in raw material. Figure 7 shows one matched pair of episodes, BF16 against INT4 on the same task; Table D decomposes the two active channels into the individual tool names and error strings that produce the aggregate rates; and Figure 8 shows what the reflexive repair loop does to the same failure mode, in the one cell where it is individually significant.
